title: Production Costs, Market and Value Chain Management in Crops and Livestock

lessons.title: Understanding production costs
lessons.html:
Understanding production costs

A farmer can only make sound decisions by knowing what each enterprise costs and earns. Costs are grouped to support different decisions.

Types of costs

TypeExamplesBehaviour
Variable (directly allocated) costsSeed, fertiliser, chemicals, fuel, feed, licks, vet costs, casual labour, marketing and transportChange with the size of the enterprise
Fixed (overhead) costsPermanent wages, insurance, depreciation, interest, rates, adminDo not change much in the short term

Gross margin

Gross margin = gross production value minus directly allocated variable costs. It is the main tool to compare enterprises.

Example (maize, per hectare): yield 5 t at R3 800 per tonne gives gross value R19 000. Variable costs of R13 500 leave a gross margin of R5 500 per hectare. This figure must also cover fixed costs and profit.

Break-even analysis

  • Break-even yield = total cost per hectare divided by price per tonne. Using the example and adding R3 000 of fixed costs per hectare: R16 500 divided by R3 800 is about 4.3 t/ha.
  • Break-even price = total cost per hectare divided by expected yield: R16 500 divided by 5 t is R3 300 per tonne.

These help decide whether to plant, how to price forward contracts and how much risk is acceptable.

Livestock costs

For a cow-calf herd, calculate gross margin per cow or per large stock unit: weaner and cull sales minus feed, licks, animal health, marketing and replacement costs. Feed is usually the largest variable cost in intensive livestock systems.

Record keeping

Keep records per enterprise and per land or camp. Use accounting or farm management software where possible, and reconcile physical records (tonnes, head) with financial records.

lessons.title: Markets and value chains
lessons.html:
Markets and value chains

Market channels

ProductMain channels
Grain and oilseedsSilo owners and traders, millers, feed mills; prices linked to the JSE commodity derivatives market
WeanersFeedlots (direct or via agents), auctions
Slaughter stockAbattoirs, butcheries, auctions
Fresh produceMunicipal fresh produce markets via market agents, retailers, exporters, informal traders
Wool and mohairBrokers and auctions
MilkProcessors, own processing

Price risk management

  • Forward contracts with a buyer fix price and quantity before harvest.
  • Futures and options on the JSE allow hedging grain prices, usually through a broker.
  • Spreading sales over time reduces the risk of selling everything at the lowest price.
  • Use break-even prices to decide when a contract price is acceptable.

The value chain

A value chain includes input suppliers, producers, transporters, storers, processors, wholesalers, retailers and consumers. Each link adds cost and value. Farmers who understand the chain can:

  • meet buyer specifications (grade, size, certification, traceability) to earn premiums;
  • reduce transaction costs by collective marketing through co-operatives or producer groups;
  • capture more value by storage, processing or direct selling where it pays;
  • build long-term relationships with reliable buyers.

Market information

Follow market reports, auction results, fresh produce market prices, exchange rates and input price trends. Rand weakness raises imported input costs (fertiliser, chemicals, fuel) and often grain prices.

Contracts and compliance

Read contracts carefully: quality specifications, delivery terms, penalties, payment terms. Meet legal requirements for grading, labelling, livestock identification and meat safety where applicable.

Key points

  • Separate variable and fixed costs; use gross margins to compare enterprises.
  • Calculate break-even yields and prices before committing.
  • Choose market channels that match product, scale and quality.
  • Manage price risk with forward contracts, hedging and spread sales.
  • Meet buyer specifications and use collective marketing to capture value.
